Case 5:25-cv-00851-EJD        Document 63        Filed 09/29/25      Page 1 of 7




                                   1

                                   2

                                   3

                                   4                                   UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   5                                  NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   6                                          SAN JOSE DIVISION

                                   7

                                   8        GOOGLE IRELAND LIMITED,                          Case No. 5:25-cv-00851-EJD
                                                         Plaintiff,                          ORDER DENYING MOTION TO
                                   9
                                                                                             INTERVENE
                                                    v.
                                  10

                                  11        OOO GOOGLE,                                      Re: ECF No. 43
                                                         Defendant.
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13            In a transparent attempt to avoid this Court’s jurisdiction, Defendant OOO Google

                                  14   (“Google Russia”) made the decision to not appear and to not defend itself against Plaintiff

                                  15   Google Ireland Limited’s (“Google Ireland”) lawsuit. At the same time, one of its allies—NO

                                  16   Fond Pravoslavnogo Televideniya (“Pravoslav”)—moved to blunt the consequences of that

                                  17   strategic default by seeking to intervene and defend against the lawsuit in Google Russia’s place.

                                  18   But Pravoslav lacks standing to intervene. And even if Pravoslav did have standing, it has not

                                  19   shown that it is entitled to intervene as of right, nor that permissive intervention is warranted

                                  20   considering Google Russia’s strategic decision. Therefore, the Court DENIES the motion to

                                  21   intervene.

                                  22   I.       BACKGROUND
                                  23            This case grows out of a long running dispute between Google LLC (“Google”)—

                                  24   including its international affiliates, Google Ireland and Google Russia—and various Russian

                                  25   media companies.1 The dispute began in July 2020, when Google terminated the accounts of one

                                  26
                                  27   1
                                        Another case stemming from this same dispute is also before this Court. See Google LLC v.
                                  28   NAO Tsargrad Media, No. 5:24-cv-5423 (N.D. Cal.).
                                       Case No.: 5:25-cv-00851-EJD
                                       ORDER DEN. MOT. TO INTERVENE                 1
                                            Case 5:25-cv-00851-EJD        Document 63       Filed 09/29/25      Page 2 of 7




                                   1   such company, NAO Tsargrad Media. Andreatta Decl. ¶ 11, ECF No. 5-2. According to Google,

                                   2   it did so to comply with U.S. sanctions law and in response to violations of its own policies. Id.

                                   3   Tsargrad viewed the terminations as unjustified, so one month later it sued Google, Google

                                   4   Ireland, and Google Russia in Russian court. Radin Decl., Ex. 4, ECF No. 5-5.2 The Russian

                                   5   court entered judgment in Tsargrad’s favor, and that judgment was affirmed on appeal. Radin

                                   6   Decl., Exs. 5–7, ECF Nos. 5-6, 5-7, 5-8. Later, Pravoslav and other Russian media companies

                                   7   secured similar judgments. Iliasova Decl. ¶¶ 16–19, ECF No. 43-2.

                                   8           To enforce Tsargrad’s judgment, Russian authorities subsequently seized $100 million of

                                   9   Google Russia’s assets, even though Tsargrad’s judgment sat at about $12.5 million at the time of

                                  10   seizure. Radin Decl. ¶¶ 4, 6–7, ECF No. 5-1. This forced Google Russia into bankruptcy. Radin

                                  11   Decl., Ex. 8, ECF No. 5-9. A Russian bankruptcy court then appointed Valeriy Talyarovsky as

                                  12   Google Russia’s liquidator, passing full control of Google Russia to Talyarovsky. Radin Decl.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   ¶ 12. Exercising this control and acting on behalf of Google Russia, Talyarovsky filed two

                                  14   adversary claims against Google Ireland in Russian bankruptcy court. With its first claim, Google

                                  15   Russia sought to rescind two agreements between itself and Google Ireland, thereby clawing back

                                  16   $1.3 billion in payments that it had made to Google Ireland. Radin Decl., Ex. 11, ECF No. 5-12.

                                  17   With its second, Google Russia sought to extend secondary liability for its debts to Google Ireland

                                  18   and other Google entities and employees. Radin Decl., Ex. 10, ECF No. 5-11.

                                  19           Google Ireland filed suit in this Court to enjoin the adversary proceedings in Russian

                                  20   bankruptcy court on these two claims, and to compel those claims to arbitration. ECF No. 1.

                                  21   Concurrently, Google Ireland moved for a temporary restraining order (“TRO”). ECF No. 5. The

                                  22   Court granted a TRO (later converted to a preliminary injunction) which, in relevant part, enjoined

                                  23   Google Russia from seeking an anti-suit injunction in Russian court. ECF Nos. 18 (“TRO”), 37

                                  24   (converting TRO to preliminary injunction). But Google Russia ignored the Court’s order. The

                                  25

                                  26   2
                                         The Court cites to various Russian court documents submitted with Google Ireland’s earlier
                                  27   motion for a temporary restraining order. See Radin Decl., Exs. 3–11. Those exhibits are subject
                                       to judicial notice. Color Switch LLC v. Fortafy Games DMCC, 377 F. Supp. 3d 1075, 1089 n.6
                                  28   (E.D. Cal. 2019).
                                       Case No.: 5:25-cv-00851-EJD
                                       ORDER DEN. MOT. TO INTERVENE                    2
                                          Case 5:25-cv-00851-EJD           Document 63        Filed 09/29/25      Page 3 of 7




                                   1   day after being served the Court’s TRO, Google Russia asked a Russian court for anti-suit

                                   2   injunctions. ECF No. 24. The Russian court granted the request and enjoined Google Ireland

                                   3   from pursuing this action. ECF Nos. 32, 51, 61.

                                   4          As the Russian injunction illustrates, Google Russia is well aware of this case. Yet Google

                                   5   Russia has not appeared in this matter. Instead, Pravoslav appeared to defend against Google

                                   6   Ireland’s claims as a third party. Pravoslav first tried to submit an amicus brief in support of

                                   7   Google Russia. ECF No. 31. When the Court denied that motion, Pravoslav moved to formally

                                   8   intervene for the purpose of vacating the injunction by relying on its status as one of Google

                                   9   Russia’s judgment creditors. Mot., ECF No. 43; Iliasova Decl. ¶¶ 16–19. The motion to intervene

                                  10   is currently before the Court.

                                  11   II.    DISCUSSION
                                  12          A.      Standing
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          Because Google Russia has failed to appear, Pravoslav is the only party seeking to defend

                                  14   against the claims in this matter. As the only party seeking to appear on the defense side,

                                  15   Pravoslav must “independently fulfill[] the requirements of Article III” standing in order to

                                  16   intervene. Wittman v. Personhuballah, 578 U.S. 539, 544 (2016) (internal quotations and citations

                                  17   omitted). That is, Pravoslav must show it (1) suffered an injury-in-fact that is (2) fairly traceable

                                  18   to this litigation and that (3) will likely be redressed by a favorable ruling. Id. at 543 (quoting

                                  19   Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 560–61 (1992)).

                                  20          In bankruptcy and bankruptcy-adjacent proceedings, a party generally has Article III

                                  21   standing where it “holds a financial stake in the outcome of the proceeding such that the [party]

                                  22   has an appropriate incentive to participate in an adversarial form to protect his or her interests.” In

                                  23   re Thorpe Insulation Co., 677 F.3d 869, 887 (9th Cir. 2012) (citation omitted). Pravoslav has such

                                  24   a financial stake here in the form of its claim against Google Russia’s bankruptcy estate. Iliasova

                                  25   Decl. ¶¶ 16–19. In the abstract, a restriction on Google Russia’s ability to increase the value of its

                                  26   bankruptcy estate would be an injury to Pravoslav’s interest because it limits what Pravoslav may

                                  27   recover from the bankruptcy estate. In re Brower, 651 B.R. 770, 776 (N.D. Cal. 2023). The

                                  28   Court’s injunction preventing Google Russia from prosecuting its adversary claims in Russian
                                       Case No.: 5:25-cv-00851-EJD
                                       ORDER DEN. MOT. TO INTERVENE                   3
                                            Case 5:25-cv-00851-EJD         Document 63        Filed 09/29/25       Page 4 of 7




                                   1   courts is such a restriction and constitutes injury-in-fact under Article III. However, that injury is

                                   2   neither fairly traceable to this litigation nor redressable by ruling in favor of Pravoslav.

                                   3           Traceability and redressability are usually distinct concepts. The former refers to the

                                   4   causal connection between the challenged conduct and alleged injury, while the latter refers to the

                                   5   connection between the judicial relief requested and the alleged injury. Allen v. Wright, 468 U.S.

                                   6   737, 753 n.19 (1984), abrogated on other grounds by Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static Control

                                   7   Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014). In this case, the challenged conduct and requested relief

                                   8   are the same: Pravoslav challenges the preliminary injunction and requests that it be vacated. As

                                   9   such, traceability and redressability3 both turn on whether the injunction here caused Pravoslav’s

                                  10   alleged injury. On this record, the answer is no.

                                  11           To be sure, the bar for redressability is low. As the Supreme Court recently held, simply

                                  12   removing a “barrier” between the plaintiff and the outcome she seeks can satisfy redressability.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Gutierrez v. Saenz, 145 S. Ct. 2258, 2268 (2025). The Court’s injunction in this case poses, at

                                  14   least in theory, a “barrier” between Pravoslav its hoped-for outcome—that Google Russia will

                                  15   prevail in Russian bankruptcy court and increase the value of its bankruptcy estate. But theory is

                                  16   all this argument amounts to. Google Russia has ignored the Court’s injunction and continued to

                                  17   pursue its adversary claims in Russian bankruptcy court. ECF Nos. 32, 51, 61. Vacating the

                                  18   injunction will change nothing at all about how Google Russia is prosecuting its claims and thus

                                  19   will have no impact on the likelihood that Pravoslav’s injury will be redressed.

                                  20           For this reason alone, the Court must deny Pravoslav’s motion.

                                  21           B.     Rule 24
                                  22           Even if Pravoslav had standing to intervene, it has not shown that intervention is

                                  23   appropriate under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24.

                                  24                  1.      Intervention as of Right
                                  25           A party may intervene as of right under Rule 24(a)(2) if it “(i) timely moves to intervene;

                                  26
                                  27   3
                                         Since traceability merges into redressability under these circumstances, the Court refers only to
                                  28   redressability for the remainder of this Order.
                                       Case No.: 5:25-cv-00851-EJD
                                       ORDER DEN. MOT. TO INTERVENE                      4
                                          Case 5:25-cv-00851-EJD           Document 63         Filed 09/29/25       Page 5 of 7




                                   1   (ii) has a significantly protectable interest related to the subject of the action; (iii) may have that

                                   2   interest impaired by the disposition of the action; and (iv) will not be adequately represented by

                                   3   existing parties.” Oakland Bulk & Oversized Terminal, LLC v. City of Oakland, 960 F.3d 603,

                                   4   620 (9th Cir. 2020). There is no dispute that Pravoslav’s motion was timely. Pravoslav filed just

                                   5   two weeks after the Court entered a preliminary injunction and in accordance with the Court’s

                                   6   deadlines. See ECF Nos. 37, 39. It is equally clear that Pravoslav is not adequately represented

                                   7   by any existing party since the only defendant, Google Russia, has not made an appearance. The

                                   8   only issue is whether Pravoslav’s interest in this case is “significantly protectable.” The Court

                                   9   finds it is not.

                                  10           A “significantly protectable interest” is a “practical impairment of its interests as a result of

                                  11   the pending litigation.” California ex rel. Lockyer v. United States, 450 F.3d 436, 441 (9th Cir.

                                  12   2006); Wilderness Soc. v. U.S. Forest Serv., 630 F.3d 1173, 1179 (9th Cir. 2011); Sierra Club v.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   U.S. E.P.A., 995 F.2d 1478, 1484 (9th Cir. 1993). While Pravoslav’s interest in Google Russia’s

                                  14   bankruptcy estate suffices for Article III injury, Rule 24 requires more. The Ninth Circuit has

                                  15   made clear that “an allegedly impaired ability to collect judgments arising from past claims does

                                  16   not, on its own, support a right to intervention.” United States v. Alisal Water Corp., 370 F.3d

                                  17   915, 920 (9th Cir. 2004). Yet Pravoslav’s purported interest is just that. Pravoslav contends it has

                                  18   a significantly protectable interest in preventing Google Ireland from interfering with the Court

                                  19   Liquidator and Russian court proceedings because it is “first in line” to be paid for its claims from

                                  20   any recovery obtained. To succeed on this theory, Pravoslav would also need to show that the

                                  21   interest in the prospective collectability of debt is “sufficiently related” to the action here. Id. at

                                  22   920–21 (finding the proposed intervenor’s “interest in the prospective collectability of the debt . . .

                                  23   [was] not sufficiently related to the environmental enforcement action brought by the United

                                  24   States”). But this action concerns only where and how Google Russia may bring its claims against

                                  25   Google Ireland; Google Ireland does not seek to recover or prevent the recovery of the total assets

                                  26   available. The Court therefore finds that Pravoslav’s interest in the collectability of debt is not

                                  27   sufficiently related to this action. See Glyn v. Roy Al Boat Mgmt. Corp., 897 F. Supp. 451, 453

                                  28   (D. Haw. 1995) (“Were this court to agree that Efimov could intervene . . . it would transform
                                       Case No.: 5:25-cv-00851-EJD
                                       ORDER DEN. MOT. TO INTERVENE                    5
                                            Case 5:25-cv-00851-EJD          Document 63          Filed 09/29/25   Page 6 of 7




                                   1   every civil suit before this court into a kind of exaggerated interpleader action where all potential

                                   2   creditors of all parties could assert their rights.”).

                                   3            The cases Pravoslav cites to the contrary are unavailing or inapplicable. See California

                                   4   Dep't of Toxic Substances Control v. Jim Dobbas, Inc., 54 F.4th 1078 (9th Cir. 2022) (allowing

                                   5   insurance company to intervene on behalf of its insured in a lawsuit it had the duty to defend);

                                   6   Westchester Fire Ins. Co. v. Mendez, 585 F.3d 1183 (9th Cir. 2009)4 (same); Twitch Interactive,

                                   7   Inc. v. Fishwoodco GmbH, No. 5:22-CV-03218-EJD, 2023 WL 7458374, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 9,

                                   8   2023) (finding action to confirm arbitration award sufficiently tied to intervener because the award

                                   9   would bind them as well); Ocean Thermal Energy Corp. v. Coe, No. LACV19-05299-VAP-JPR,

                                  10   2020 WL 4108161, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Mar. 5, 2020) (finding action to enforce the sale of assets

                                  11   sufficiently tied to intervenor because the sale would directly prevent intervenor from collecting

                                  12   debt).
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13            C.     Permissive Intervention
                                  14            Courts also have the discretion to allow permissive intervention. “Under Federal Rule of

                                  15   Civil Procedure 24(b), a district court has discretion to permit intervention when the movant

                                  16   presents (1) an independent ground for jurisdiction; (2) a timely motion; and (3) a common

                                  17   question of law and fact between the movant’s claim or defense and the main action.” Callahan v.

                                  18   Brookdale Senior Living Communities, Inc., 42 F.4th 1013, 1022 (9th Cir. 2022) (internal

                                  19   quotation marks omitted) (quoting Freedom from Religion Found., Inc. v. Geithner, 644 F.3d 836,

                                  20   843 (9th Cir. 2011)). If the proposed intervenor satisfies these requirements, then courts may

                                  21   consider several additional discretionary factors, including: the nature and extent of the

                                  22   intervenors’ interest; whether the intervenor has standing; whether intervention will prolong or

                                  23   unduly delay the litigation; and whether intervention would contribute “to the just and equitable

                                  24   adjudication” of the case. Id. (quoting Spangler v. Pasadena City Bd. of Educ., 552 F.2d 1326,

                                  25   1329 (9th Cir. 1977)).

                                  26            Pravoslav fails to satisfy all the necessary requirements. Though Pravoslav filed a timely

                                  27
                                       4
                                        Pravoslav appears to cite to two separate cases named “Westchester” and “Mendez,” but the
                                  28   Court finds only one citation in its brief including both names.
                                       Case No.: 5:25-cv-00851-EJD
                                       ORDER DEN. MOT. TO INTERVENE                       6
                                          Case 5:25-cv-00851-EJD           Document 63        Filed 09/29/25      Page 7 of 7




                                   1   motion, for the reasons discussed above, it has not established jurisdiction or a common question

                                   2   of law and fact between the Pravoslav’s claim and this action. And even if Pravoslav satisfied

                                   3   these requirements, the Court would exercise its discretion to deny permissive intervention.

                                   4   Google Russia has intentionally defaulted. Pravoslav suggests that Google Russia’s default can be

                                   5   excused because Google Russia would need to request permission from the Russian bankruptcy

                                   6   court to hire U.S. counsel to defend itself; but there is no indication that Google Russia ever asked

                                   7   the bankruptcy court for permission. Instead, Google Russia immediately sought an anti-suit

                                   8   injunction after the Court issued its own injunction here, indicating its intent to proceed in its

                                   9   Russian case while ignoring this case. The Court will not reward Google Russia’s intentional

                                  10   default by allowing it to enlist an ally to defend this case on the merits. Such an intervention

                                  11   would frustrate “the just and equitable adjudication” of this case. Id.

                                  12   III.   CONCLUSION
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          Based on the foregoing, the Court DENIES the motion to intervene (ECF No. 40) and

                                  14   accompanying motions for leave to appear in Pro Hac Vice (ECF Nos. 46, 47).

                                  15          IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                  16   Dated: September 29, 2025

                                   4                                   UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   5                                  NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   7

                                   8        GOOGLE IRELAND LIMITED,                         Case No. 5:25-cv-00851-EJD
                                                         Plaintiff,                         ORDER GRANTING MOTION FOR

                                                                                            DEFAULT JUDGMENT
                                                   v.
                                  10

                                  11        OOO GOOGLE,                                     Re: ECF No. 43
                                                         Defendant.
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13            Defendant OOO Google (“Google Russia”) has made the decision to not appear in this

                                  14   action.1 After giving it numerous opportunities to appear and respond, the Court ordered the Clerk

                                  15   of Court to enter default against Google Russia on April 3, 2025. ECF No. 55. The Court then

                                  16   provided Google Russia one final chance to appear by filing an appearance on the docket or

                                  17   moving to vacate the default by April 24, 2025. Id. Google Russia has not done so. It is now

                                  18   September. As the Court indicated in its prior order, the Court will now consider Plaintiff Google

                                  19   Ireland Limited’s (“Google Ireland”) motion at ECF No. 5, as well as the automatic conversion

                                  20   provision of the preliminary injunction, as a motion for default judgment. ECF No. 55.

                                  21            For the reasons explained below, the Court ENTERS DEFAULT JUDGMENT against

                                  22   Google Russia and in favor of Google Ireland.

                                  23   I.       LEGAL STANDARD
                                  24            Courts may grant default judgment if a party fails to plead or otherwise defend against an

                                  25   action for affirmative relief. Fed. R. Civ. P. 55(a). Discretion to enter default judgment rests with

                                  26
                                  27   1
                                         The Court incorporates the facts as described in its concurrently filed Order Denying the Motion
                                       to Intervene.
                                  28   Case No.: 5:25-cv-00851-EJD
                                       ORDER ENTERING DEFAULT JUDGMENT
                                                                                        1
                                            Case 5:25-cv-00851-EJD        Document 64        Filed 09/29/25       Page 2 of 5




                                   1   the district court. Aldabe v. Aldabe, 616 F.2d 1089, 1092 (9th Cir. 1980). Prior to entering default

                                   2   judgment, courts must (1) examine subject matter jurisdiction and personal jurisdiction, In re

                                   3   Tulli, 172 F.3d 707, 712 (9th Cir. 1999), and (2) consider the factors described in Eitel v. McCool,

                                   4   782 F.2d 1470, 1471–72 (9th Cir. 1986).

                                   5   II.     DISCUSSION
                                   6           A.     Jurisdiction
                                   7           The Court finds it has subject-matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to 9 U.S.C. § 4

                                   8   and personal jurisdiction over Google Russia pursuant to its agreement to arbitrate all disputes

                                   9   relating to the RSAs in Santa Clara County, California. Compl. ¶¶ 11, 13, ECF No. 1. The Court

                                  10   further finds Google Ireland has Article III standing to bring this suit. Google Russia’s litigation

                                  11   has forced Google Ireland to litigate in a forum other than the one agreed to by the parties, and an

                                  12   order compelling arbitration and issuing a permanent anti-suit injunction would redress this injury.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992).2

                                  14           B.     Eitel Factors
                                  15           Next, the Court finds the Eitel factors weigh in favor of granting default judgment. Under

                                  16   Eitel, courts consider the following:

                                  17                  (1) the possibility of prejudice to the plaintiff, (2) the merits of
                                                      plaintiff's substantive claim, (3) the sufficiency of the complaint, (4)
                                  18                  the sum of money at stake in the action, (5) the possibility of a dispute
                                                      concerning material facts, (6) whether the underlying default was due
                                  19                  to excusable neglect, and (7) the strong policy underlying the Federal
                                                      Rules of Civil Procedure favoring decisions on the merits.
                                  20

                                  21
                                       2
                                         Google Russia is deemed to have waived all defenses upon entry of default. See Rubicon Glob.
                                  22   Ventures, Inc. v. Chongquing Zongshen Grp. Imp./Exp. Corp., 630 F. App'x 655, 657–68 (9th Cir.
                                       2015); Innovative Health Techs. v. Urmeev, No. CV-18-03372-PHX-ROS, 2020 WL 4346751, at
                                  23   *3 n.3 (D. Ariz. July 29, 2020). However, because the Court has an independent obligation to
                                       evaluate Article III standing, the Court has considered and rejected Proposed Intervenor
                                  24   Pravoslav’s arguments regarding standing. The Court finds Google Russia is the proper party
                                       because it is the signatory to the relevant contract—the fact that the Russian Liquidator is suing in
                                  25   Russia rather than Google Russia is irrelevant since the Liquidator is acting as Google Russia’s
                                       agent. There is also clearly a controversy because Google Russia is refusing to arbitrate even after
                                  26   being served a demand. Finally, the prior exclusive jurisdiction doctrine does not apply here
                                       because, although bankruptcy proceedings are generally in rem, this is a contract dispute, which is
                                  27   the archetypical in personam action. See Silk v. Bond, 65 F.4th 445 (9th Cir. 2023); Va. Cmty.
                                       Coll. v. Katz, 546 U.S. 356, 371–72 (2006).

                                       ORDER ENTERING DEFAULT JUDGMENT
                                                                                         2
                                         Case 5:25-cv-00851-EJD           Document 64        Filed 09/29/25       Page 3 of 5




                                   1   Eitel, 782 F.2d at 1471–72. In evaluating these factors, all factual allegations in the complaint are

                                   2   taken as true, except those relating to damages. TeleVideo Sys., Inc. v. Heidenthal, 826 F.2d 915,

                                   3   917–18 (9th Cir. 1987).

                                   4          Under the first Eitel factor, courts consider whether plaintiffs will suffer prejudice if

                                   5   default judgment is denied. Bd. of Trustees, I.B.E.W. Local 332 Pension Plan Part A v. Delucchi

                                   6   Elec., Inc., No. 5:19-CV-06456-EJD, 2020 WL 2838801, at *2 (N.D. Cal. June 1, 2020) (citing

                                   7   PepsiCo, Inc. v. Cal. Security. Cans, 238 F. Supp. 2d 1172, 1177 (C.D. Cal. 2002)). A plaintiff is

                                   8   prejudiced if it would be “without other recourse for recovery” because the defendant failed to

                                   9   appear or defend against the suit. JL Audio, Inc. v. Kazi, No. 516CV00785CASJEM, 2017 WL

                                  10   4179875, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Sept. 18, 2017). Because Google Russia has not appeared in this

                                  11   matter, Google Ireland will be without any other recourse for recovery unless default judgment is

                                  12   granted. Oomph Innovations LLC v. Shenzhen Bolsesic Elecs. Co., No. 5:18-cv-05561-EJD, 2020
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   WL 5847505, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 30, 2020).

                                  14          The second and third Eitel factors are often examined together. I.B.E.W. Local 332, 2020

                                  15   WL 2838801, at *2 (citing PepsiCo, 238 F. Supp. 2d at 1175). These factors assess the

                                  16   substantive merits of the movant’s claims and the sufficiency of the pleadings. PepsiCo, 238 F.

                                  17   Supp. 2d at 1175. In its TRO, the Court already found Google Ireland has pled facts sufficient to

                                  18   show a likelihood of success on the merits under the Rule 65 standard. For those same reasons,

                                  19   the Court finds Google Ireland has satisfied these factors by stating a claim on which it may

                                  20   recover.

                                  21          As to the fourth factor, “[w]hen the money at stake in the litigation is substantial or

                                  22   unreasonable, default judgment is discouraged.” Bd. of Trustees v. Core Concrete Cost., Inc., No.

                                  23   C 11-02532 LB, 2012 WL 380304, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 17, 2012), report and recommendation

                                  24   adopted, 2012 WL 381198 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 6, 2012). There is no request for monetary relief here

                                  25   apart from attorneys’ fees.

                                  26          Regarding the possibility of a dispute concerning material facts, Google Russia has neither

                                  27   appeared nor defended this action, and Google Ireland’s allegations stand undisputed. See Shaw v.

                                  28   Case No.: 5:25-cv-00851-EJD
                                       ORDER ENTERING DEFAULT JUDGMENT
                                                                                        3
                                          Case 5:25-cv-00851-EJD           Document 64          Filed 09/29/25   Page 4 of 5




                                   1   Five M, LLC, No. 16-cv-03955-BLF, 2017 WL 747465, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 27, 2017) (noting

                                   2   that upon entry of default by the Clerk of the Court, the factual allegations of the complaint related

                                   3   to liability are taken as true). The Court therefore finds that the possibility of dispute concerning

                                   4   material facts is minimal and does not weigh against default judgment. Oomph Innovations, No.

                                   5   5:18-cv-05561-EJD, 2020 WL 5847505, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 30, 2020).

                                   6            Moving to considerations of excusable neglect, for the reasons stated in the Court’s Order

                                   7   Denying the Motion for Intervention, there is no indication of excusable neglect; indeed, the Court

                                   8   finds Google Russia’s default is knowing and intentional.

                                   9            Finally, although public policy strongly favors deciding each case on its merits, default

                                  10   judgment is appropriate where a defendant refuses to litigate a case and where default judgment is

                                  11   the plaintiff's only recourse against the defendant. See Core Concrete, 2012 WL 380304, at *4;

                                  12   Carlson Produce, LLC v. Clapper, No. 18-cv-07195-VKD, 2020 WL 533004, at *5 (N.D. Cal.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Feb. 3, 2020); see also United States v. Roof Guard Roofing Co., No. 17-cv-02592-NC, 2017 WL

                                  14   6994215, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 14, 2017) (“When a properly adversarial search for the truth is

                                  15   rendered futile, default judgment is the appropriate outcome.”). Such is the case here, where

                                  16   Google Russia has not appeared and refuses to litigate. Oomph Innovations, 2020 WL 5847505,

                                  17   at *4.

                                  18            Accordingly, the Court finds all Eitel factors weigh in favor of granting default judgment.

                                  19   III.     CONCLUSION AND ORDER
                                  20            Based on the foregoing, the Court ENTERS DEFAULT JUDGMENT. The Court

                                  21   declares that the mandatory arbitration provisions in the 2009 RSA and 2018 RSA are binding

                                  22   upon Google Russia and compels arbitration in accordance with Section 12 of the 2009 RSA and

                                  23   Section 12 of the 2018 RSA.

                                  24            The Court also converts the preliminary injunction, ECF Nos. 18, 37, into a permanent

                                  25   injunction enjoining Google Russia, its Liquidator, officers, agents, servants, employees and

                                  26   attorneys, and all those in active concert or participation with them, whether acting directly or

                                  27   indirectly, in the United States or abroad, from:

                                   1              a. commencing, prosecuting, continuing, taking any steps in, or otherwise

                                   2                  participating in any proceedings to pursue or redress any claims on behalf of

                                   3                  Google Russia against Google Ireland or its current or former affiliates, or any of

                                   4                  their officers, agents, servants, employees, or attorneys, relating to the RSAs in any

                                   5                  forum other than the arbitration proceedings mandated by the terms of the RSAs;

                                   6              b. commencing, prosecuting, continuing, taking any steps in, or otherwise

                                   7                  participating in any proceedings to pursue clawback, secondary liability or other

                                   8                  claims in the Russian Federation relating to the RSAs on behalf of Google Russia

                                   9                  against Google Ireland or its current or former affiliates, or any of their officers,

                                  10                  agents, servants. employees, or attorneys, including the applications filed by

                                  11                  Google Russia’s liquidator on October 18, 2024 in the Arbitrazh Court; or

                                  12              c. commencing, prosecuting, continuing, taking any steps in, or otherwise
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13                  participating in any proceedings in the Russian Federation intended to restrain or

                                  14                  impede Google Ireland’s pursuit of this action.

                                  15           The Court further awards attorneys’ fees and costs pursuant to 47 U.S.C. §

                                  16   605(e)(3)(B)(iii) but defers ruling on the amount of fees. Google Ireland shall file a motion for

                                  17   attorneys’ fees within 14 days of this Order, including a bill of costs pursuant to Civil Local Rule

                                  18   54-1.

                                  19           IT IS SO ORDERED.
